DNT (Do-Not-Translate) Handling - [ ] **Identify DNT classes before starting**: brand/product names, trademarks, code identifiers, variable/function names, file paths, URLs, email addresses, commands, API keys, version/model numbers, legal entity names. - [ ] **Load the project glossary with DNT terms flagged** in your CAT tool (terminology recognition / locked terms); do not rely on memory alone. - [ ] **Copy DNT strings exactly**: preserve casing, spacing, hyphenation, and punctuation. No transliteration unless the glossary specifies a localized brand form for that market. - [ ] **Watch for false DNT look-alikes** — common nouns that resemble product names (e.g., "Finder," "Edge," "Swift"). - [ ] **Protect placeholders/variables** in all syntaxes: `{0}`, `%s`, `%1$s`, `%@`, `{{name}}`, `${var}`, `%d`. Never translate, reorder, or delete them; reposition them only as target grammar requires. - [ ] **Run a pseudo-localization pass** pre- and post-translation to surface leaked DNT strings (untranslated source text appearing in the build, or translated text where DNT was required) [2]. ## 2. Tag / Markup Integrity - [ ] **Preserve all inline tags**; run the CAT tool's tag-validation check before delivery. Tag count and pairing must match source even when tag *position* shifts for target word order. - [ ] **Never break nesting order** of paired tags (`……` must close in reverse order); orphan/unpaired tags are the #1 cause of build failures. - [ ] **HTML/XML**: translate only translatable attribute values (`alt`, `title`, `aria-label`, `placeholder`); never touch element names, attribute names, `id`/`class`, `href` (unless a locale-specific URL is specified), or `

message.content: # Preserving Entities, Numbers, and Markup in Localized Output ## A Research Report on Principles, Mechanisms, and Quality Enforcement --- ## Executive Summary The instruction to "preserve entities, numbers, and markup from the source passages in the localized output" encodes one of the most consequential rules in localization: **certain source content is invariant, while only its presentation may adapt to the target locale.** Failure to preserve this content is not a stylistic flaw — it is a functional defect class that breaks software builds, corrupts financial and legal data, and renders products unusable. This report synthesizes guidance from formal standards (ISO 17100:2015, ISO 18587:2017), industry bodies (GALA, TAUS, CSA Research), the MQM error taxonomy, Unicode infrastructure (CLDR, ICU MessageFormat), interoperability formats (XLIFF, W3C ITS), academic NMT research, and production QA tooling. The consistent finding across all of these sources is that preservation must be engineered at **four layers**: (1) declarative markup of what must be protected, (2) pipeline mechanisms that make protected content un-editable, (3) MT architecture that does not corrupt it, and (4) automated and human QA that catches residual violations before release. --- ## 1. The Three Preservation Classes and Why They Break ### 1.1 Named entities Brand names, product names, trademarks, person and place names, legal entity names, code identifiers, file paths, URLs, and API keys must typically survive translation untouched — or be rendered via a *documented, per-locale* transliteration decision. Unpreserved entities surface in quality evaluation as the MQM **Naming** error type ("incorrect name for a person, place, or organization") or as **Mistranslation** under Accuracy [1][2]. CSA Research positions protected naming as a brand-integrity issue: enterprises should define which names are never translated, test names per market for negative connotations and trademark conflicts, and centralize naming decisions so all vendors apply identical treatment [3]. ### 1.2 Numbers The cardinal rule, repeated across every source examined, is: **values are immutable; only formatting adapts.** A changed value (7% → 70%, 1,500 → 15,000, 1945 → 1995, 3.14 → 314) is a critical Mistranslation/Number error [1][2]; an adapted format (1,234.56 → 1.234,56) is correct locale handling. ISO 18587:2017 explicitly treats numbers, dates, and named entities as classic MT failure points that post-editors must verify even under light post-editing [4]. ### 1.3 Markup Inline tags, placeholders, and variables (`…`, `{0}`, `%s`, `%1$s`, `%@`, `{{name}}`, `${var}`, ``, ``) map to formatting, variables, and runtime behavior. MQM's **Design → Markup** category defines the failure: "target contains markup that is missing, incorrect, or does not correspond to the source markup" — e.g., unbalanced/dropped tags, a link tag around the wrong words, or "Clickhere" (missing space) [1][2]. Industry QA documentation identifies tag errors as among the most common causes of broken localized UIs and runtime crashes [5][6][7]. --- ## 2. The Governing Principle: Preserve the Value, Adapt the Format A crucial distinction runs through all authoritative sources — **preservation and localization are not opposites**: | Content | What may change | What must never change | |---|---|---| | Numbers | Separators, digit grouping, currency symbol/position, decimal digits, date order, calendar system | The numeric value itself | | Named entities | Script (per documented transliteration policy), name order conventions | The identity the name refers to | | Markup | Tag **position** (as target word order requires) | Tag **count, pairing, nesting order, and content** | Locale adaptation itself is governed by **Unicode CLDR**, the canonical locale-data repository covering **1,100+ locales**, used by ICU, Chrome, Android, Windows, macOS/iOS, Java, and .NET [8][9]. Key variation points include: - **Separators:** `1,234.56` (en) vs. `1.234,56` (de) vs. `1 234,56` (fr, narrow no-break space U+202F) vs. Arabic-Indic `١٬٢٣٤٫٥٦`; Indian 2-2-3 grouping (`1,23,45,678`); `minimumGroupingDigits=2` in es/it/pt [9][10]. - **~80 numbering systems** in CLDR (Latin, Arabic-Indic, Devanagari, Thai, Roman, Hebrew) [9][10]. - **Percent placement:** `50%` (en) vs. `50 %` (fr) vs. `%50` (tr) [10]. - **Currency:** JPY = 0 minor-unit digits, BHD/KWD = 3, most = 2; ambiguous symbols (`$`, `£`, `kr`) render as `US$` in en-CA but `$` in en-US; cash-rounding increments (e.g., CHF 0.05) [9][10]. - **Dates/calendars:** Gregorian plus Buddhist (th), Islamic, Persian (fa), Hebrew, Japanese imperial eras, Chinese lunar, Minguo; field order varies (`MMMM d, y` en-US; `d. MMMM y` de; `y年M月d日` ja) — never hardcode order or slice formatted strings [9][11]. - **Hour cycles** h11/h12 vs. h23/h24; first day of week; week-numbering rules [9][11]. ### 2.1 Plural rules: the hidden numeric trap CLDR defines up to **six plural categories** — `zero, one, two, few, many, other` — selected by rules over operands `n, i, v, w, f, t, e` [9][10]. Japanese/Chinese/Korean/Thai/Vietnamese use only `other`; English uses `one/other`; **Russian** uses `one/few/many/other` (1, 21… vs. 2–4, 22–24… vs. 0, 5–20…); **Arabic and Welsh use all six**; Irish uses five; **French has a `many`** category for large round numbers ("un million **d'**habitants") [10]. The engineering implication is absolute: code must use ICU `PluralRules`/MessageFormat — never `n == 1 ? "item" : "items"` — and translators must supply *every* category variant. GNU gettext encodes the same logic as per-language `Plural-Forms` expressions (`nplurals=3` for Russian) [12]. --- ## 3. Declarative Protection: Marking What Must Not Be Translated ### 3.1 W3C Internationalization Tag Set (ITS) **ITS 1.0** (W3C Recommendation, April 2007) defines six data categories — Translate, Localization Note, Terminology, Directionality, Language Information, Elements Within Text — via global rules (`its:rules` with XPath selectors) or local attributes [13]. **ITS 2.0** (W3C Recommendation, October 2013) adds ten more (16 total), including Domain, Text Analysis, Locale Filter, Preserve Space, Localization Quality Issue, and Provenance, with native HTML5 support (`translate`/`dir` attributes, `its-*` local attributes) [14]. Its practical effect: tools can **declaratively identify translatable vs. protected content** (e.g., `translate="no"`, script blocks, terminology) upstream of translation. ### 3.2 DNT lists and termbases (GALA / ISO 17100) GALA's guidance centers on **linguistic asset management**: build termbases with approved, banned, and conditional terms validated with client SMEs before kickoff; maintain **"Do Not Translate" (DNT) lists** for brand names, product names, trademarks, UI strings, and code identifiers; decide per locale whether proper nouns stay in source script or are transliterated — and record the decision [15]. ISO 17100:2015 mandates that terminology/glossaries, style guides, and reference materials be agreed **before production begins**, that client-supplied termbases be used with gaps flagged, and that source ambiguities (inconsistent names, unclear numbers) be **queried to the client rather than silently "corrected"** [16]. --- ## 4. Structural Carriers: XLIFF Inline Tags and ICU MessageFormat ### 4.1 XLIFF **XLIFF 1.2** (OASIS, February 2008) embeds five inline elements in ``/``: ``/`` (paired native codes, matched via `rid`/`id`), `` (standalone placeholder), `` (isolated begin/end), and `` (translatable content inside a code), with `ctype` and `equiv-text` attributes [17]. **XLIFF 2.x** (2.0 in 2014; 2.1 in 2019; 2.2 in 2020) redesigns the model: ``, `` (paired code containing content), ``/``, ``/``; native codes stored out-of-line in `` referenced by `dataRef`; and behavior controls — **`canCopy`, `canDelete`, `canReorder`** — that machine-enforce what a translator may do with a tag [18][19][20]. Android `strings.xml` embeds `` tags to mark non-translatable string parts [18]. ### 4.2 CAT-tool placeholder protection Format filters convert native markup — HTML/XML tags, printf (`%s`, `%1$s`), .NET (`{0}`), Java/ICU (`{name}`), Apple (`%@`), `${var}` — into **atomic inline tokens before segmentation**, so tokens are never split and translators cannot edit inside them. Typical protections: locked tags, insertion via shortcut, open/close pairing enforcement, auto-propagation, and QA verification for missing, extra, reordered, or empty tags (Trados Studio tag verification, memoQ QA, OmegaT validation, Phrase tag QA, Crowdin/Lokalise variable highlighting) [5][6][7]. ### 4.3 ICU MessageFormat **MessageFormat 1** syntax `{arg, type, style}` supports `number`, `date`, `time`, `spellout`, `ordinal`, `duration`, plus plural/select with CLDR categories and `#` for the formatted number [21]. **MessageFormat 2** — tech preview in ICU 75 (2024), **stable in ICU 76 (October 2024)** — adds declarations (`.input`, `.local`), `.match` selection, function placeholders (`{$count :number style=integer}`), defined error/fallback behavior, and **first-class markup parts** (open/close placeholders) so inline tags can be represented without breaking message syntax [22][23]. --- ## 5. MT Pipelines: Why Models Corrupt Preserved Content and How They Are Fixed ### 5.1 Documented failure modes - **Numbers:** Early NMT mapped rare tokens to ``; Luong et al. (2015) categorized rare-word errors (names, numbers) and showed post-hoc fixes recovering up to **≈ +2.8 BLEU** on WMT'14 [24]. BPE subword models (Sennrich et al., 2016) solved open vocabulary but split digit strings into **arbitrary fragments → dropped, duplicated, or mistranslated digits**, with verbatim copying even where locale conventions differ [25][26]. Koehn & Knowles (2017) listed rare words among six persistent NMT challenges [26]; Spithourakis & Riedel (2018) confirmed digit sequences are poorly modeled without format-aware treatment [27]. - **Names:** UNK omission, hallucination, inconsistent transliteration, or copying when an established target-language exonym exists; strong sensitivity to character-level noise (Belinkov & Bisk, 2018) [26][28]. - **Markup:** Models trained on plain text **delete, duplicate, misorder, or misnest tags** and corrupt placeholders; long-range reordering makes positional preservation hard [2][29]. ### 5.2 Architectural mitigations The literature converges on a layered recipe [24][25][29][30]: 1. **Copy/pointer mechanisms** — CopyNet (Gu et al., 2016), pointer-softmax (Gulcehre et al., 2016), pointer-generator (See et al., 2017); Umugwaneza et al. (AFRICON 2023) showed copy-augmented models improve retention of named entities, numbers, and OOV words for Kinyarwanda→English [31][32][33][34]. 2. **NER-driven placeholder masking** — detect entities, replace with type-tagged unique placeholders, re-insert after translation; Bunk et al. (2019) reported BLEU gains and fewer entity errors for English→German; Hoang et al. (2018) used entity masking during back-translation to force copying [35][36]. 3. **Hard terminology constraints** — lexically constrained decoding (Hokamp & Liu 2017; Post & Vilar 2018) and training models to apply glossaries via placeholder-style tokens (Dinu et al., 2019) [37][38][39]. 4. **Retrieval** — kNN-MT (Khandelwal et al., 2021) improves rare-token and entity consistency from translation memories [40]. 5. **Numeric post-validation** — no architectural fix fully eliminates digit and markup errors [27][2]. ### 5.3 Commercial-engine features Production engines operationalize these ideas as **glossaries/DNT enforcement** (Google Cloud Translation, Microsoft Translator, DeepL, ModernMT) — the pipeline-level equivalent of the DNT lists and constrained decoding described above [15][37][39]. --- ## 6. Enforcement: QA Workflows That Catch Violations ### 6.1 Automated QA checks Automated QA runs on bilingual files or TMS segments, flagging mechanical errors [5][6][7]: - **Tag/formatting mismatch** — missing, extra, duplicated, or reordered inline tags between source and target. - **Number mismatch** — compares numeric values source vs. target to catch dropped, altered, or mistranslated figures; advanced checkers **normalize for locale conventions** (decimal comma vs. point, digit grouping) to reduce false positives. - **Additional checks** — untranslated segments, source=target, terminology violations, forbidden characters, whitespace, capitalization, punctuation, URL/email integrity, length limits. Standard tools: **XBench** (de-facto industry standard, free), Trados Studio QA Checker, memoQ QA, Verifika, QA Distiller, and built-in QA in cloud TMS platforms (Phrase, Smartling, Crowdin, Lokalise, Transifex). Checks run (a) continuously as translators type, (b) as a gate before delivery to reviewers, and (c) as a final pre-release batch check, with errors triaged as real vs. false positive and re-run until zero critical errors remain [5][6][7]. ### 6.2 MQM: making preservation auditable The **Multidimensional Quality Metrics** framework makes preservation failures countable via explicit issue types [1][2][41]: | Failure | Full MQM tree | MQM 2021 revision | |---|---|---| | Wrong entity | Accuracy → Mistranslation; Locale convention → Person names | **Naming**: "incorrect name for a person, place, or organization" | | Wrong value | Accuracy → Mistranslation | **Number**: "numbers that do not match the source" | | Wrong format only | Locale convention → Number format | Locale convention | | Broken tags | Design → **Markup** | Design | **Severity is orthogonal to category**: Critical (renders text unusable; risk of physical, financial, legal, or reputational harm), Major (significantly disrupts comprehension/usability), Minor (detracts but does not impede), Neutral (zero penalty). Widely used default penalty weights are **Minor = 1, Major = 5, Critical = 25**; the WMT MQM protocol scores Minor = 1, Major = 5, treating Critical errors as extremely rare [41][42][43]. TAUS's Dynamic Quality Framework contributes a harmonized typology with matching categories (terminology, accuracy, locale convention) [44]. ### 6.3 Human LQA and sampling LQA is performed by a second linguist — the ISO 17100:2015 **two-person workflow** requires every translation to be checked by a second qualified linguist, explicitly covering accuracy, completeness, and terminology consistency [16]. Reviewers annotate errors with type and severity, apply weighted deductions, and compute a score (pass thresholds commonly around **95–99 points out of 100**); critical errors may trigger automatic failure regardless of total score. Because full review is expensive, LQA often uses sampling, with 100% review reserved for high-risk content (legal, medical, UI strings shipped to millions of users). Results feed back into training, glossary/style-guide updates, and MT post-editing rules [41][43][44]. ### 6.4 Pseudo-localization and regression testing Pseudo-locales machine-transform source strings **before real translations exist** [45][46][47]: - **Accented pseudo** (`en-XA`): maps ASCII to accented/exotic characters — reveals encoding bugs, missing glyphs, hardcoded strings. - **Expansion pseudo:** pads strings **~30–40% longer** (matching German/French growth), wrapped in delimiters (`[!!! Hëllô !!!]`) — reveals truncation, overflow, and **concatenation bugs** (brackets appearing mid-sentence). - **Pseudo-bidi** (`ar-XB`): substitutes RTL-looking characters and inserts directional marks — surfaces bidi/layout/mirroring bugs. Pseudo runs verify that placeholders (`{0}`, `%s`, `{{name}}`) and ICU patterns survive intact. Xcode ships Double-Length, Accented, and Right-to-Left pseudolanguages; Android exposes en-XA/ar-XB in developer options [45][47]. **Limits:** pseudo-locales still use English plural rules and don't test real Arabic shaping or Russian plural categories — complement with snapshot tests against real locales (de-DE, ar-EG, ru-RU, ja-JP, hi-IN) [45]. Post-integration regression testing verifies per-language builds: UI strings fit containers, variables render at runtime, hotkeys don't collide in translated labels, and localized resources load without missing-key errors — automated via screenshot comparison per locale, locale-parameterized UI frameworks (Selenium, Appium, Playwright), string-length assertions, and untranslated-English "leak" detection, gated in CI/CD [48][49]. --- ## 7. Consolidated Best-Practice Checklist **Named entities** - Inventory entity classes; decide keep/transliterate/translate **per locale** and record the decision [15][3]. - Store as DNT or termbase entries; load glossary with DNT flags in the CAT tool; copy strings exactly (casing, spacing, hyphenation) [15][50]. - Verify against authoritative sources; auto-check DNT strings; watch for false look-alikes ("Finder," "Edge," "Swift") [50]. **Numbers** - Adapt *format* to locale (per CLDR) but never alter *values*; diff source vs. target digit-by-digit [9][50]. - Apply correct separators, currency symbol/position/decimal digits (JPY = 0, KWD = 3); disambiguate `$` with ISO code where specified [10][50]. - Protect numbers that must not be reformatted (version numbers, serials, phone numbers, postal codes, legal references); disable autoformat interference [50]. - Use full CLDR plural categories — never concatenate number + fixed noun [10][12]. **Markup** - Preserve all inline tags; tag count and pairing must match source even when position shifts; never break nesting order — orphan tags are the #1 cause of build failures [5][50]. - Translate only translatable attribute values (`alt`, `title`, `aria-label`); never touch element/attribute names, `id`/`class`, or `

This report synthesizes guidance from formal standards (ISO 17100:2015, ISO 18587:2017), industry bodies (GALA, TAUS, CSA Research), the MQM error taxonomy, Unicode infrastructure (CLDR, ICU MessageFormat), interoperability formats (XLIFF, W3C ITS), academic NMT research, and production QA tooling. The consistent finding across all of these sources is that preservation must be engineered at **four layers**: (1) declarative markup of what must be protected, (2) pipeline mechanisms that make protected content un-editable, (3) MT architecture that does not corrupt it, and (4) automated and human QA that catches residual violations before release. --- ## 1. The Three Preservation Classes and Why They Break ### 1.1 Named entities Brand names, product names, trademarks, person and place names, legal entity names, code identifiers, file paths, URLs, and API keys must typically survive translation untouched — or be rendered via a *documented, per-locale* transliteration decision. Unpreserved entities surface in quality evaluation as the MQM **Naming** error type ("incorrect name for a person, place, or organization") or as **Mistranslation** under Accuracy [1][2]. CSA Research positions protected naming as a brand-integrity issue: enterprises should define which names are never translated, test names per market for negative connotations and trademark conflicts, and centralize naming decisions so all vendors apply identical treatment [3]. ### 1.2 Numbers The cardinal rule, repeated across every source examined, is: **values are immutable; only formatting adapts.** A changed value (7% → 70%, 1,500 → 15,000, 1945 → 1995, 3.14 → 314) is a critical Mistranslation/Number error [1][2]; an adapted format (1,234.56 → 1.234,56) is correct locale handling. ISO 18587:2017 explicitly treats numbers, dates, and named entities as classic MT failure points that post-editors must verify even under light post-editing [4]. ### 1.3 Markup Inline tags, placeholders, and variables (`…`, `{0}`, `%s`, `%1$s`, `%@`, `{{name}}`, `${var}`, ``, ``) map to formatting, variables, and runtime behavior. MQM's **Design → Markup** category defines the failure: "target contains markup that is missing, incorrect, or does not correspond to the source markup" — e.g., unbalanced/dropped tags, a link tag around the wrong words, or "Clickhere" (missing space) [1][2]. Industry QA documentation identifies tag errors as among the most common causes of broken localized UIs and runtime crashes [5][6][7]. --- ## 2. The Governing Principle: Preserve the Value, Adapt the Format A crucial distinction runs through all authoritative sources — **preservation and localization are not opposites**: | Content | What may change | What must never change | |---|---|---| | Numbers | Separators, digit grouping, currency symbol/position, decimal digits, date order, calendar system | The numeric value itself | | Named entities | Script (per documented transliteration policy), name order conventions | The identity the name refers to | | Markup | Tag **position** (as target word order requires) | Tag **count, pairing, nesting order, and content** | Locale adaptation itself is governed by **Unicode CLDR**, the canonical locale-data repository covering **1,100+ locales**, used by ICU, Chrome, Android, Windows, macOS/iOS, Java, and .NET [8][9]. MMMM y` de; `y年M月d日` ja) — never hardcode order or slice formatted strings [9][11]. - **Hour cycles** h11/h12 vs. h23/h24; first day of week; week-numbering rules [9][11]. ### 2.1 Plural rules: the hidden numeric trap CLDR defines up to **six plural categories** — `zero, one, two, few, many, other` — selected by rules over operands `n, i, v, w, f, t, e` [9][10]. Declarative Protection: Marking What Must Not Be Translated ### 3.1 W3C Internationalization Tag Set (ITS) **ITS 1.0** (W3C Recommendation, April 2007) defines six data categories — Translate, Localization Note, Terminology, Directionality, Language Information, Elements Within Text — via global rules (`its:rules` with XPath selectors) or local attributes [13]. **ITS 2.0** (W3C Recommendation, October 2013) adds ten more (16 total), including Domain, Text Analysis, Locale Filter, Preserve Space, Localization Quality Issue, and Provenance, with native HTML5 support (`translate`/`dir` attributes, `its-*` local attributes) [14]. MT Pipelines: Why Models Corrupt Preserved Content and How They Are Fixed ### 5.1 Documented failure modes - **Numbers:** Early NMT mapped rare tokens to ``; Luong et al. (2015) categorized rare-word errors (names, numbers) and showed post-hoc fixes recovering up to **≈ +2.8 BLEU** on WMT'14 [24]. BPE subword models (Sennrich et al., 2016) solved open vocabulary but split digit strings into **arbitrary fragments → dropped, duplicated, or mistranslated digits**, with verbatim copying even where locale conventions differ [25][26]. Koehn & Knowles (2017) listed rare words among six persistent NMT challenges [26]; Spithourakis & Riedel (2018) confirmed digit sequences are poorly modeled without format-aware treatment [27]. - **Names:** UNK omission, hallucination, inconsistent transliteration, or copying when an established target-language exonym exists; strong sensitivity to character-level noise (Belinkov & Bisk, 2018) [26][28]. - **Markup:** Models trained on plain text **delete, duplicate, misorder, or misnest tags** and corrupt placeholders; long-range reordering makes positional preservation hard [2][29]. ### 5.2 Architectural mitigations The literature converges on a layered recipe [24][25][29][30]: 1. **Copy/pointer mechanisms** — CopyNet (Gu et al., 2016), pointer-softmax (Gulcehre et al., 2016), pointer-generator (See et al., 2017); Umugwaneza et al. (AFRICON 2023) showed copy-augmented models improve retention of named entities, numbers, and OOV words for Kinyarwanda→English [31][32][33][34]. 2. **NER-driven placeholder masking** — detect entities, replace with type-tagged unique placeholders, re-insert after translation; Bunk et al. (2019) reported BLEU gains and fewer entity errors for English→German; Hoang et al. (2018) used entity masking during back-translation to force copying [35][36]. 3. **Hard terminology constraints** — lexically constrained decoding (Hokamp & Liu 2017; Post & Vilar 2018) and training models to apply glossaries via placeholder-style tokens (Dinu et al., 2019) [37][38][39]. 4. **Retrieval** — kNN-MT (Khandelwal et al., 2021) improves rare-token and entity consistency from translation memories [40]. 5. **Numeric post-validation** — no architectural fix fully eliminates digit and markup errors [27][2]. ### 5.3 Commercial-engine features Production engines operationalize these ideas as **glossaries/DNT enforcement** (Google Cloud Translation, Microsoft Translator, DeepL, ModernMT) — the pipeline-level equivalent of the DNT lists and constrained decoding described above [15][37][39]. --- ## 6. Enforcement: QA Workflows That Catch Violations ### 6.1 Automated QA checks Automated QA runs on bilingual files or TMS segments, flagging mechanical errors [5][6][7]: - **Tag/formatting mismatch** — missing, extra, duplicated, or reordered inline tags between source and target. - **Number mismatch** — compares numeric values source vs. target to catch dropped, altered, or mistranslated figures; advanced checkers **normalize for locale conventions** (decimal comma vs. point, digit grouping) to reduce false positives. - **Additional checks** — untranslated segments, source=target, terminology violations, forbidden characters, whitespace, capitalization, punctuation, URL/email integrity, length limits. Widely used default penalty weights are **Minor = 1, Major = 5, Critical = 25**; the WMT MQM protocol scores Minor = 1, Major = 5, treating Critical errors as extremely rare [41][42][43]. TAUS's Dynamic Quality Framework contributes a harmonized typology with matching categories (terminology, accuracy, locale convention) [44]. ### 6.3 Human LQA and sampling LQA is performed by a second linguist — the ISO 17100:2015 **two-person workflow** requires every translation to be checked by a second qualified linguist, explicitly covering accuracy, completeness, and terminology consistency [16]. Reviewers annotate errors with type and severity, apply weighted deductions, and compute a score (pass thresholds commonly around **95–99 points out of 100**); critical errors may trigger automatic failure regardless of total score. Because full review is expensive, LQA often uses sampling, with 100% review reserved for high-risk content (legal, medical, UI strings shipped to millions of users). Results feed back into training, glossary/style-guide updates, and MT post-editing rules [41][43][44]. ### 6.4 Pseudo-localization and regression testing Pseudo-locales machine-transform source strings **before real translations exist** [45][46][47]: - **Accented pseudo** (`en-XA`): maps ASCII to accented/exotic characters — reveals encoding bugs, missing glyphs, hardcoded strings. - **Expansion pseudo:** pads strings **~30–40% longer** (matching German/French growth), wrapped in delimiters (`[!!! Hëllô !!!]`) — reveals truncation, overflow, and **concatenation bugs** (brackets appearing mid-sentence). - **Pseudo-bidi** (`ar-XB`): substitutes RTL-looking characters and inserts directional marks — surfaces bidi/layout/mirroring bugs. Pseudo runs verify that placeholders (`{0}`, `%s`, `{{name}}`) and ICU patterns survive intact. Xcode ships Double-Length, Accented, and Right-to-Left pseudolanguages; Android exposes en-XA/ar-XB in developer options [45][47]. **Limits:** pseudo-locales still use English plural rules and don't test real Arabic shaping or Russian plural categories — complement with snapshot tests against real locales (de-DE, ar-EG, ru-RU, ja-JP, hi-IN) [45]. Typical protections: locked tags, insertion via shortcut, open/close pairing enforcement, auto-propagation, and QA verification for missing, extra, reordered, or empty tags (Trados Studio tag verification, memoQ QA, OmegaT validation, Phrase tag QA, Crowdin/Lokalise variable highlighting) [5][6][7]. ### 4.3 ICU MessageFormat **MessageFormat 1** syntax `{arg, type, style}` supports `number`, `date`, `time`, `spellout`, `ordinal`, `duration`, plus plural/select with CLDR categories and `#` for the formatted number [21]. **MessageFormat 2** — tech preview in ICU 75 (2024), **stable in ICU 76 (October 2024)** — adds declarations (`.input`, `.local`), `.match` selection, function placeholders (`{$count :number style=integer}`), defined error/fallback behavior, and **first-class markup parts** (open/close placeholders) so inline tags can be represented without breaking message syntax [22][23]. --- ## 5. MT Pipelines: Why Models Corrupt Preserved Content and How They Are Fixed ### 5.1 Documented failure modes - **Numbers:** Early NMT mapped rare tokens to ``; Luong et al. (2015) categorized rare-word errors (names, numbers) and showed post-hoc fixes recovering up to **≈ +2.8 BLEU** on WMT'14 [24]. BPE subword models (Sennrich et al., 2016) solved open vocabulary but split digit strings into **arbitrary fragments → dropped, duplicated, or mistranslated digits**, with verbatim copying even where locale conventions differ [25][26]. Koehn & Knowles (2017) listed rare words among six persistent NMT challenges [26]; Spithourakis & Riedel (2018) confirmed digit sequences are poorly modeled without format-aware treatment [27]. - **Names:** UNK omission, hallucination, inconsistent transliteration, or copying when an established target-language exonym exists; strong sensitivity to character-level noise (Belinkov & Bisk, 2018) [26][28]. - **Markup:** Models trained on plain text **delete, duplicate, misorder, or misnest tags** and corrupt placeholders; long-range reordering makes positional preservation hard [2][29]. ### 5.2 Architectural mitigations The literature converges on a layered recipe [24][25][29][30]: 1. **Copy/pointer mechanisms** — CopyNet (Gu et al., 2016), pointer-softmax (Gulcehre et al., 2016), pointer-generator (See et al., 2017); Umugwaneza et al. (AFRICON 2023) showed copy-augmented models improve retention of named entities, numbers, and OOV words for Kinyarwanda→English [31][32][33][34]. 2. **NER-driven placeholder masking** — detect entities, replace with type-tagged unique placeholders, re-insert after translation; Bunk et al. (2019) reported BLEU gains and fewer entity errors for English→German; Hoang et al. (2018) used entity masking during back-translation to force copying [35][36]. 3. **Hard terminology constraints** — lexically constrained decoding (Hokamp & Liu 2017; Post & Vilar 2018) and training models to apply glossaries via placeholder-style tokens (Dinu et al., 2019) [37][38][39]. 4. **Retrieval** — kNN-MT (Khandelwal et al., 2021) improves rare-token and entity consistency from translation memories [40]. 5. **Numeric post-validation** — no architectural fix fully eliminates digit and markup errors [27][2]. ### 5.3 Commercial-engine features Production engines operationalize these ideas as **glossaries/DNT enforcement** (Google Cloud Translation, Microsoft Translator, DeepL, ModernMT) — the pipeline-level equivalent of the DNT lists and constrained decoding described above [15][37][39]. --- ## 6. Enforcement: QA Workflows That Catch Violations ### 6.1 Automated QA checks Automated QA runs on bilingual files or TMS segments, flagging mechanical errors [5][6][7]: - **Tag/formatting mismatch** — missing, extra, duplicated, or reordered inline tags between source and target. - **Number mismatch** — compares numeric values source vs. target to catch dropped, altered, or mistranslated figures; advanced checkers **normalize for locale conventions** (decimal comma vs. point, digit grouping) to reduce false positives. - **Additional checks** — untranslated segments, source=target, terminology violations, forbidden characters, whitespace, capitalization, punctuation, URL/email integrity, length limits. Standard tools: **XBench** (de-facto industry standard, free), Trados Studio QA Checker, memoQ QA, Verifika, QA Distiller, and built-in QA in cloud TMS platforms (Phrase, Smartling, Crowdin, Lokalise, Transifex). Checks run (a) continuously as translators type, (b) as a gate before delivery to reviewers, and (c) as a final pre-release batch check, with errors triaged as real vs. false positive and re-run until zero critical errors remain [5][6][7]. ### 6.2 MQM: making preservation auditable The **Multidimensional Quality Metrics** framework makes preservation failures countable via explicit issue types [1][2][41]: | Failure | Full MQM tree | MQM 2021 revision | |---|---|---| | Wrong entity | Accuracy → Mistranslation; Locale convention → Person names | **Naming**: "incorrect name for a person, place, or organization" | | Wrong value | Accuracy → Mistranslation | **Number**: "numbers that do not match the source" | | Wrong format only | Locale convention → Number format | Locale convention | | Broken tags | Design → **Markup** | Design | **Severity is orthogonal to category**: Critical (renders text unusable; risk of physical, financial, legal, or reputational harm), Major (significantly disrupts comprehension/usability), Minor (detracts but does not impede), Neutral (zero penalty). Widely used default penalty weights are **Minor = 1, Major = 5, Critical = 25**; the WMT MQM protocol scores Minor = 1, Major = 5, treating Critical errors as extremely rare [41][42][43]. TAUS's Dynamic Quality Framework contributes a harmonized typology with matching categories (terminology, accuracy, locale convention) [44]. ### 6.3 Human LQA and sampling LQA is performed by a second linguist — the ISO 17100:2015 **two-person workflow** requires every translation to be checked by a second qualified linguist, explicitly covering accuracy, completeness, and terminology consistency [16]. Reviewers annotate errors with type and severity, apply weighted deductions, and compute a score (pass thresholds commonly around **95–99 points out of 100**); critical errors may trigger automatic failure regardless of total score. Because full review is expensive, LQA often uses sampling, with 100% review reserved for high-risk content (legal, medical, UI strings shipped to millions of users). Results feed back into training, glossary/style-guide updates, and MT post-editing rules [41][43][44]. ### 6.4 Pseudo-localization and regression testing Pseudo-locales machine-transform source strings **before real translations exist** [45][46][47]: - **Accented pseudo** (`en-XA`): maps ASCII to accented/exotic characters — reveals encoding bugs, missing glyphs, hardcoded strings. - **Expansion pseudo:** pads strings **~30–40% longer** (matching German/French growth), wrapped in delimiters (`[!!! Hëllô !!!]`) — reveals truncation, overflow, and **concatenation bugs** (brackets appearing mid-sentence). - **Pseudo-bidi** (`ar-XB`): substitutes RTL-looking characters and inserts directional marks — surfaces bidi/layout/mirroring bugs. Pseudo runs verify that placeholders (`{0}`, `%s`, `{{name}}`) and ICU patterns survive intact. Xcode ships Double-Length, Accented, and Right-to-Left pseudolanguages; Android exposes en-XA/ar-XB in developer options [45][47]. **Limits:** pseudo-locales still use English plural rules and don't test real Arabic shaping or Russian plural categories — complement with snapshot tests against real locales (de-DE, ar-EG, ru-RU, ja-JP, hi-IN) [45]. Post-integration regression testing verifies per-language builds: UI strings fit containers, variables render at runtime, hotkeys don't collide in translated labels, and localized resources load without missing-key errors — automated via screenshot comparison per locale, locale-parameterized UI frameworks (Selenium, Appium, Playwright), string-length assertions, and untranslated-English "leak" detection, gated in CI/CD [48][49]. --- ## 7. # Brazilian Portuguese (pt-BR) Formatting Conventions

## Numbers
- **Decimal separator:** comma — `3,14`
- **Thousands separator:** period — `1.234.567,89`
- Grouping is in threes; no special grouping for 4-digit years, postal codes, etc.
- Number words use the **short scale**: *mil* (10³), *milhão* (10⁶), *bilhão* (10⁹), *trilhão* (10¹²) [1][3]
- CLDR decimal pattern: `#,##0.###` with `latn` (Western) digits [1]

## Currency (BRL — Brazilian Real)
- **Symbol:** `R$` (ISO 4217: BRL, numeric 986); subunit *centavos* (1/100) [4]
- **Placement:** symbol **before** the amount, separated by a (non-breaking) space — `R$ 1.234,56` [1][4]
- CLDR pattern: `¤ #,##0.00` → renders as `R$ 1.234,56` [1]
- The space is standard in official usage (Banco Central do Brasil, major style guides); informal writing sometimes omits it, but implementations should keep it [4]
- Typographic note: the Brazilian *cifrão* is traditionally drawn with two strokes, but in plain text/Unicode it is simply `R$` [1]

## Negative Numbers
- Standard: **minus sign prefix** — `-1.234,56`
- Negative currency per CLDR: pattern `-¤ #,##0.00` → `-R$ 1.234,56` (minus before the symbol) [1]
- Parenthesized negatives `(R$ 1.234,56)` appear only in some accounting spreadsheets/reports; they are **not** the locale standard [1][3]
- Some software renders `R$ -1.234,56`; this is a variant, not CLDR-conformant [1]

## Percent
- Sign **follows** the number, **no space** — `50%`, `12,5%` [1][3]
- CLDR patterns: `#,##0%` (positive), `-%,##0%`-style negative → `-50%` [1]
- Financial rates often add qualifiers: `12,5% a.a.` (per year), `1,2% a.m.` (per month) [4]

## Implementation Summary (CLDR/ICU pt-BR)
| Item | Value |
|---|---|
| Decimal | `,` |
| Group | `.` |
| Decimal pattern | `#,##0.###` |
| Currency pattern | `¤ #,##0.00` |
| Negative currency | `-¤ #,##0.00` |
| Percent pattern | `#,##0%` |

## Sources
[1] Unicode CLDR, locale data for pt-BR (patterns, separators, currency/percent formats) — cldr.unicode.org
[2] ICU (International Components for Unicode) locale documentation — unicode-org.github.io/icu
[3] Microsoft Go-Global / Windows locale reference for Portuguese (Brazil)
[4] Banco Central do Brasil — official currency usage and BRL specifications (bcb.gov.br)

# Brazilian Portuguese (pt-BR) Date & Time Conventions

## Date patterns

| Style | Pattern | Example (2026-09-25) |
|---|---|---|
| Short | dd/MM/yyyy | 25/09/2026 |
| Medium | d 'de' MMM 'de' yyyy | 25 de set. de 2026 |
| Long | d 'de' MMMM 'de' yyyy | 25 de setembro de 2026 |
| Full | EEEE, d 'de' MMMM 'de' yyyy | sexta-feira, 25 de setembro de 2026 |

- The day/month/year order with slashes is the universal everyday format; the "de" connectors are required in written-out dates [1][4].
- Cardinal numbers are used for the day (dia 25, not "vigésimo quinto"); month and weekday names are lowercase in running text [1].

## Time formats

- CLDR standard patterns for pt-BR are 24-hour: short **HH:mm**, medium **HH:mm:ss**; full/long use the characteristic notation **HH'h'mm'mm'ss'ss'** (e.g., 14h30min25s) plus zone [1][4].
- The "h" separator (14h30, 9h15min) is the dominant convention in Brazilian writing.
- In everyday speech, the 12-hour clock with qualifiers is common ("às 3 da tarde", "9 da manhã"), but formal/technical formatting is 24-hour [1][4].

## First day of week

- **Sunday (domingo)** is the first day of the week in Brazil (CLDR week data: BR = sun) [2].
- Consequently Monday is *segunda-feira* ("second day"), through Friday *sexta-feira*; Saturday and Sunday are *sábado* and *domingo*.

## Month and weekday names

- **Months:** janeiro, fevereiro, março, abril, maio, junho, julho, agosto, setembro, outubro, novembro, dezembro. Abbreviated: jan., fev., mar., abr., mai., jun., jul., ago., set., out., nov., dez. [1]
- **Weekdays:** domingo, segunda-feira, terça-feira, quarta-feira, quinta-feira, sexta-feira, sábado. Abbreviated: dom., seg., ter., qua., qui., sex., sáb. [1]

## ISO 8601 usage

- Brazil has adopted ISO 8601 as a national standard via **ABNT NBR ISO 8601** (latest edition aligned with ISO 8601-1:2019) [3]. The YYYY-MM-DD format is standard in technical, scientific, IT, and data-exchange contexts.
- ABNT bibliographic style (NBR 6023) writes dates as "25 set. 2026" in citations [3].
- In daily life, dd/mm/yyyy prevails; ISO format is not used colloquially.

## Related notes

- **Time zone:** Brasília Time (BRT, UTC−3) is the de facto national reference; the country spans UTC−2 (Fernando de Noronha) to UTC−5. **Daylight saving time was abolished in 2019** by federal decree [5].
- Decimal comma / thousands point apply to numeric formatting generally [4].

**Sources:** [1] Unicode CLDR pt-BR locale data (date/time patterns) · [2] CLDR Supplemental Week Data (territory first-day) · [3] ABNT NBR ISO 8601 / NBR 6023 standards · [4] Microsoft Windows locale documentation (pt-BR) · [5] Decreto federal nº 9.772/2019 (extinção do horário de verão)

# Gender-Inclusive & Non-Binary Language in Brazilian Portuguese (pt-BR) Localization

## 1. Why pt-BR is a hard case
Brazilian Portuguese is a strongly gendered language: articles, nouns, adjectives, and past participles all inflect for masculine/feminine (e.g., *o usuário registrado / a usuária registrada*). There is no standardized grammatical neuter, so all neutralization strategies are either (a) rephrasing with genderless words, (b) non-standard neologisms, or (c) generic masculine (grammatically standard but increasingly contested) [1][3][6].

## 2. 'x' and '@' endings
- **Forms:** *todxs, bem-vindx, amigx* (x-endings) and *tod@s, amig@s* (@-endings). The '@' form emerged first (1990s–2000s feminist/LGBTQ+ print and digital activism); 'x' became dominant in online spaces in the 2010s.
- **Pronunciation:** Neither has a settled spoken form. '@' is read aloud as "arroba" (e.g., "tod-arroba"); 'x' is read as "xis" or variously proposed as /us/ ("todus"). This mismatch between written and spoken form is a core criticism.
- **Accessibility:** Screen readers (NVDA, JAWS, VoiceOver) read '@' as "arroba" and 'x' as "xis", breaking comprehension for blind users — a concern documented repeatedly in Brazilian accessibility writing [7][9].
- **Style guide stance:** Major corporate pt-BR style guides (Microsoft, Google) do **not** use '@'/'x' endings in product UI or documentation; they are treated as non-standard and harmful to readability, terminology consistency, and text-to-speech. They may appear only in community/marketing contexts or when quoting [1][3][4].
- **Political context:** "Linguagem neutra" is legally contested in Brazil — several states/municipalities passed laws (2023–2024) restricting it in public schools, so public-sector-facing content requires care.

## 3. The 'elu' neopronoun
- **Paradigm (most widespread variant):** subject *elu*; possessive/oblique *delu* (variants: *dolu, ile, sol/sola*); plural *elus/delus*. Verb agreement is normally 3rd-person singular: *"Elu está aqui, trouxe delu livro"*.
- **Recognition:** Covered extensively by Brazilian media from ~2020; added to the Aulete dictionary (2021) and, per 2023 news coverage, to the Michaelis online dictionary — both moves generated public debate [8].
- **Localization practice:** 'elu' is common in community-facing content, social media, and some brand campaigns, but is **not** used in mainstream product UI by Microsoft or Google; standard practice for known non-binary individuals (users, personas, testimonials) is to respect their stated pronoun, otherwise rephrase to avoid pronouns entirely [1][3][7].

## 4. Neutral alternatives actually used in pt-BR
- ***Pessoa* constructions:** *a pessoa usuária, a pessoa desenvolvedora, as pessoas clientes* — widely adopted in Brazilian tech communities and federal government plain-language guidance [6].
- **Rephrase with *quem*:** "quem usar o serviço" instead of *o usuário que usar*.
- **Direct address + imperative:** pt-BR UI naturally avoids pronouns via *você* imperatives: *"Clique em Salvar"* — fully gender-neutral and the default in UI copy [1][3].
- **Anchor agreement to a neuter-by-convention masculine noun:** *o cadastro foi concluído*, *o acesso foi liberado* (agreement attaches to *cadastro/acesso*, not to a person).
- **Fixed neutral expressions:** *Boas-vindas!* instead of *Bem-vindo(a)*; *Olá, {nome}!* instead of *Prezado(a)*.
- **Possessives are inherently neutral in Portuguese:** *seu/sua* agree with the possessed noun, not the owner — no action needed.
- **Genderless nouns:** *a equipe, a liderança, a coordenação, o grupo*.
- **Avoid:** slashes and parentheses (*o/a usuário(a)*) — flagged as clunky and screen-reader-hostile [1][3][5][9].

## 5. Style guide positions
- **Microsoft (pt-BR):** The Portuguese (Brazil) style guide published via the Microsoft Language Portal instructs writers to minimize unnecessary gender marking, prefer neutral rephrasing or *pessoa* constructions, fall back to generic masculine only when no neutral alternative works, and avoid '@'/'x' endings and slash/parenthesis forms in product text. This aligns with Microsoft's global inclusive-language rules (avoid gendered assumptions, prefer direct address) [1][2].
- **Google:** The Google Developer Documentation Style Guide mandates gender-neutral writing (singular "they" in English); pt-BR localization guidance extends this by directing localizers to avoid gendered forms when gender is unknown, prefer neutral nouns and direct address, and reject 'o(a)'/'@'/'x' constructions in documentation and UI [3][4].
- **W3C:** The W3C editorial/manual-of-style guidance commits W3C documents to inclusive language (English-centric; singular "they"), with per-language adaptation delegated to translation teams. W3C accessibility material is the key pt-BR-relevant source: it supports the argument against '@'/'x' forms on screen-reader grounds, and W3C guidance on forms favors self-described gender fields over binary-only dropdowns [5][9].

## 6. Practical takeaways for pt-BR localization
1. Default to imperative/direct address; 2. use *pessoa usuária/pessoa cliente* or *quem*-clauses; 3. anchor agreement to neutral masculine nouns (*cadastro, acesso, item*); 4. never ship '@'/'x' endings in product text; 5. respect stated pronouns (including *elu*) for real people and personas, but don't introduce 'elu' into general UI copy; 6. avoid *bem-vindo(a)*, *prezado(a)*, and slash/parenthesis gender pairs.

## Sources
[1] Microsoft Language Portal — Portuguese (Brazil) Style Guide (microsoft.com/language)
[2] Microsoft Writing Style Guide, "Inclusive language" (learn.microsoft.com)
[3] Google Developer Documentation Style Guide (developers.google.com/style)
[4] Google localization style guide for Portuguese–Brazil (vendor-facing)
[5] W3C Editorial Style Guide / Manual of Style, "Inclusive language" (w3.org)
[6] *Guia de Comunicação em Linguagem Simples*, Governo Federal do Brasil (2023)
[7] *Guia de Mídia*, Aliança Nacional LGBTI+ (2021) — pronoun coverage incl. *elu*
[8] News coverage of Aulete (2021) and Michaelis (2023) adding "elu"
[9] Brazilian accessibility writing (e.g., Hand Talk) on screen readers and neutral language

**Caveat:** These are named primary documents rather than live search results; style guides are updated frequently, so verify exact current wording at the linked sources before citing in deliverables.

# Gender-Inclusive & Non-Binary Language in Brazilian Portuguese (pt-BR) Localization

## 1. Why pt-BR is a hard case
Brazilian Portuguese is a strongly gendered language: articles, nouns, adjectives, and past participles all inflect for masculine/feminine (e.g., *o usuário registrado / a usuária registrada*). There is no standardized grammatical neuter, so all neutralization strategies are either (a) rephrasing with genderless words, (b) non-standard neologisms, or (c) generic masculine (grammatically standard but increasingly contested) [1][3][6].

## 2. 'x' and '@' endings
- **Forms:** *todxs, bem-vindx, amigx* (x-endings) and *tod@s, amig@s* (@-endings). The '@' form emerged first (1990s–2000s feminist/LGBTQ+ print and digital activism); 'x' became dominant in online spaces in the 2010s.
- **Pronunciation:** Neither has a settled spoken form. '@' is read aloud as "arroba" (e.g., "tod-arroba"); 'x' is read as "xis" or variously proposed as /us/ ("todus"). This mismatch between written and spoken form is a core criticism.
- **Accessibility:** Screen readers (NVDA, JAWS, VoiceOver) read '@' as "arroba" and 'x' as "xis", breaking comprehension for blind users — a concern documented repeatedly in Brazilian accessibility writing [7][9].
- **Style guide stance:** Major corporate pt-BR style guides (Microsoft, Google) do **not** use '@'/'x' endings in product UI or documentation; they are treated as non-standard and harmful to readability, terminology consistency, and text-to-speech. They may appear only in community/marketing contexts or when quoting [1][3][4].
- **Political context:** "Linguagem neutra" is legally contested in Brazil — several states/municipalities passed laws (2023–2024) restricting it in public schools, so public-sector-facing content requires care.

## 3. The 'elu' neopronoun
- **Paradigm (most widespread variant):** subject *elu*; possessive/oblique *delu* (variants: *dolu, ile, sol/sola*); plural *elus/delus*. Verb agreement is normally 3rd-person singular: *"Elu está aqui, trouxe delu livro"*.
- **Recognition:** Covered extensively by Brazilian media from ~2020; added to the Aulete dictionary (2021) and, per 2023 news coverage, to the Michaelis online dictionary — both moves generated public debate [8].
- **Localization practice:** 'elu' is common in community-facing content, social media, and some brand campaigns, but is **not** used in mainstream product UI by Microsoft or Google; standard practice for known non-binary individuals (users, personas, testimonials) is to respect their stated pronoun, otherwise rephrase to avoid pronouns entirely [1][3][7].

## 4. Neutral alternatives actually used in pt-BR
- ***Pessoa* constructions:** *a pessoa usuária, a pessoa desenvolvedora, as pessoas clientes* — widely adopted in Brazilian tech communities and federal government plain-language guidance [6].
- **Rephrase with *quem*:** "quem usar o serviço" instead of *o usuário que usar*.
- **Direct address + imperative:** pt-BR UI naturally avoids pronouns via *você* imperatives: *"Clique em Salvar"* — fully gender-neutral and the default in UI copy [1][3].
- **Anchor agreement to a neuter-by-convention masculine noun:** *o cadastro foi concluído*, *o acesso foi liberado* (agreement attaches to *cadastro/acesso*, not to a person).
- **Fixed neutral expressions:** *Boas-vindas!* instead of *Bem-vindo(a)*; *Olá, {nome}!* instead of *Prezado(a)*.
- **Possessives are inherently neutral in Portuguese:** *seu/sua* agree with the possessed noun, not the owner — no action needed.
- **Genderless nouns:** *a equipe, a liderança, a coordenação, o grupo*.
- **Avoid:** slashes and parentheses (*o/a usuário(a)*) — flagged as clunky and screen-reader-hostile [1][3][5][9].

## 5. Style guide positions
- **Microsoft (pt-BR):** The Portuguese (Brazil) style guide published via the Microsoft Language Portal instructs writers to minimize unnecessary gender marking, prefer neutral rephrasing or *pessoa* constructions, fall back to generic masculine only when no neutral alternative works, and avoid '@'/'x' endings and slash/parenthesis forms in product text. This aligns with Microsoft's global inclusive-language rules (avoid gendered assumptions, prefer direct address) [1][2].
- **Google:** The Google Developer Documentation Style Guide mandates gender-neutral writing (singular "they" in English); pt-BR localization guidance extends this by directing localizers to avoid gendered forms when gender is unknown, prefer neutral nouns and direct address, and reject 'o(a)'/'@'/'x' constructions in documentation and UI [3][4].
- **W3C:** The W3C editorial/manual-of-style guidance commits W3C documents to inclusive language (English-centric; singular "they"), with per-language adaptation delegated to translation teams. W3C accessibility material is the key pt-BR-relevant source: it supports the argument against '@'/'x' forms on screen-reader grounds, and W3C guidance on forms favors self-described gender fields over binary-only dropdowns [5][9].

## 6. Practical takeaways for pt-BR localization
1. Default to imperative/direct address; 2. use *pessoa usuária/pessoa cliente* or *quem*-clauses; 3. anchor agreement to neutral masculine nouns (*cadastro, acesso, item*); 4. never ship '@'/'x' endings in product text; 5. respect stated pronouns (including *elu*) for real people and personas, but don't introduce 'elu' into general UI copy; 6. avoid *bem-vindo(a)*, *prezado(a)*, and slash/parenthesis gender pairs.

## Sources
[1] Microsoft Language Portal — Portuguese (Brazil) Style Guide (microsoft.com/language)
[2] Microsoft Writing Style Guide, "Inclusive language" (learn.microsoft.com)
[3] Google Developer Documentation Style Guide (developers.google.com/style)
[4] Google localization style guide for Portuguese–Brazil (vendor-facing)
[5] W3C Editorial Style Guide / Manual of Style, "Inclusive language" (w3.org)
[6] *Guia de Comunicação em Linguagem Simples*, Governo Federal do Brasil (2023)
[7] *Guia de Mídia*, Aliança Nacional LGBTI+ (2021) — pronoun coverage incl. *elu*
[8] News coverage of Aulete (2021) and Michaelis (2023) adding "elu"
[9] Brazilian accessibility writing (e.g., Hand Talk) on screen readers and neutral language

**Caveat:** These are named primary documents rather than live search results; style guides are updated frequently, so verify exact current wording at the linked sources before citing in deliverables.

## 1. Why pt-BR is a hard case
Brazilian Portuguese is a strongly gendered language: articles, nouns, adjectives, and past participles all inflect for masculine/feminine (e.g., *o usuário registrado / a usuária registrada*). There is no standardized grammatical neuter, so all neutralization strategies are either (a) rephrasing with genderless words, (b) non-standard neologisms, or (c) generic masculine (grammatically standard but increasingly contested) [1][3][6].

## 2. 'x' and '@' endings
- **Forms:** *todxs, bem-vindx, amigx* (x-endings) and *tod@s, amig@s* (@-endings). The '@' form emerged first (1990s–2000s feminist/LGBTQ+ print and digital activism); 'x' became dominant in online spaces in the 2010s.
- **Pronunciation:** Neither has a settled spoken form. '@' is read aloud as "arroba" (e.g., "tod-arroba"); 'x' is read as "xis" or variously proposed as /us/ ("todus"). This mismatch between written and spoken form is a core criticism.
- **Accessibility:** Screen readers (NVDA, JAWS, VoiceOver) read '@' as "arroba" and 'x' as "xis", breaking comprehension for blind users — a concern documented repeatedly in Brazilian accessibility writing [7][9].
- **Style guide stance:** Major corporate pt-BR style guides (Microsoft, Google) do **not** use '@'/'x' endings in product UI or documentation; they are treated as non-standard and harmful to readability, terminology consistency, and text-to-speech. They may appear only in community/marketing contexts or when quoting [1][3][4].
- **Political context:** "Linguagem neutra" is legally contested in Brazil — several states/municipalities passed laws (2023–2024) restricting it in public schools, so public-sector-facing content requires care.

## 3. The 'elu' neopronoun
- **Paradigm (most widespread variant):** subject *elu*; possessive/oblique *delu* (variants: *dolu, ile, sol/sola*); plural *elus/delus*. Verb agreement is normally 3rd-person singular: *"Elu está aqui, trouxe delu livro"*.
- **Recognition:** Covered extensively by Brazilian media from ~2020; added to the Aulete dictionary (2021) and, per 2023 news coverage, to the Michaelis online dictionary — both moves generated public debate [8].
- **Localization practice:** 'elu' is common in community-facing content, social media, and some brand campaigns, but is **not** used in mainstream product UI by Microsoft or Google; standard practice for known non-binary individuals (users, personas, testimonials) is to respect their stated pronoun, otherwise rephrase to avoid pronouns entirely [1][3][7].

## 4. Neutral alternatives actually used in pt-BR
- ***Pessoa* constructions:** *a pessoa usuária, a pessoa desenvolvedora, as pessoas clientes* — widely adopted in Brazilian tech communities and federal government plain-language guidance [6].
- **Rephrase with *quem*:** "quem usar o serviço" instead of *o usuário que usar*.
- **Direct address + imperative:** pt-BR UI naturally avoids pronouns via *você* imperatives: *"Clique em Salvar"* — fully gender-neutral and the default in UI copy [1][3].

- **Fixed neutral expressions:** *Boas-vindas!* instead of *Bem-vindo(a)*; *Olá, {nome}!* instead of *Prezado(a)*.
- **Possessives are inherently neutral in Portuguese:** *seu/sua* agree with the possessed noun, not the owner — no action needed.
- **Genderless nouns:** *a equipe, a liderança, a coordenação, o grupo*.
- **Avoid:** slashes and parentheses (*o/a usuário(a)*) — flagged as clunky and screen-reader-hostile [1][3][5][9].

## 5. Style guide positions
- **Microsoft (pt-BR):** The Portuguese (Brazil) style guide published via the Microsoft Language Portal instructs writers to minimize unnecessary gender marking, prefer neutral rephrasing or *pessoa* constructions, fall back to generic masculine only when no neutral alternative works, and avoid '@'/'x' endings and slash/parenthesis forms in product text. # Brazilian Portuguese (pt-BR) Localization Conventions

## 1. Measurement Units
- Brazil uses the **metric system (SI)**: metro (m), quilograma (kg), litro (L), quilômetro (km), grau Celsius (°C) [1][2].
- Fuel economy in **km/L**; land area in hectares (ha); body height in meters/centimeters (1,75 m), weight in kg.
- Notable exceptions: TV screens and tire sizes are commonly expressed in **polegadas (inches)** [2].
- Numbers use **comma as decimal separator, period as thousands separator**: 1.234,56 kg [1].

## 2. Phone Number Formats
- Country code **+55**; area codes (DDD) are two digits, written in parentheses: (11), (21) [4].
- **Mobile numbers: 9 digits** starting with 9 → (11) 91234-5678. **Landlines: 8 digits** starting with 2–5 → (11) 2345-6789 [4].
- International format: +55 11 91234-5678. International dialing: 00 + carrier code (e.g., 0021, 0015) [4].
- Special ranges: toll-free **0800 NNN NNNN**; local-rate 3003-XXXX / 4004-XXXX; emergency 190 (police), 192 (ambulance), 193 (fire) [4].

## 3. Address Formats
- Order: **street type + street name, house number, complement, bairro (neighborhood), CEP + city – state (UF)** [5].
- Example: `Av. Paulista, 1578 – Bela Vista, São Paulo – SP, 01310-200, Brasil` [5].
- Street types: Rua, Avenida (Av.), Praça, Alameda, Travessa, Rodovia; "s/n" indicates no house number [5].
- **CEP = 8 digits, NNNNN-NNN** (São Paulo starts with 0, Rio with 2, Brasília with 7) [5]. UF codes: SP, RJ, MG, BA, RS, DF, etc. [5].

## 4. Name Order
- Given name(s) + **mother's surname + father's surname** (paternal surname last, used as the primary surname) [2][3].
- Married women may append the spouse's surname; middle surnames are abbreviated (José A. Silva) [2].
- Sorting/formal lists use the final surname; titles: Sr., Sra., Srta., Dr., Dra. [2].

## 5. Sorting / Collation
- 26-letter Latin alphabet (**K, W, Y included** since the 2009 orthographic agreement) [1][6].
- Accented characters (á, ã, ç, ê, ó…) sort as their **base letters** — accents are secondary differences; ç collates as c [1].
- Digraphs ch, lh, ss are **not** treated as separate letters [1]. CLDR pt-BR collation matches the root Latin standard [1].

## 6. Quotation Marks and Punctuation

# Grammatical Gender Agreement in Portuguese — Research Summary

**Sources:** [1] Cunha & Cintra, *Nova Gramática do Português Contemporâneo* · [2] Bechara, *Moderna Gramática Portuguesa* · [3] Perini, *Modern Portuguese: A Reference Grammar* (2002) · [4] Whitlam, *Modern Brazilian Portuguese Grammar* · [5] Azevedo, *Portuguese: A Linguistic Introduction* · [6] Ciberdúvidas da Língua Portuguesa (ISCTE-IUL) · [7] *Dicionário Houaiss*

## 1. Noun gender (masculine/feminine) [1][3][7]
- Portuguese has **no neuter**; every noun is masculine or feminine, often by form:
  - **Masculine:** most **-o** words (*o livro*); Greek-origin **-ma** (*o problema, o sistema, o idioma, o clima*); most **-or** (*o escritor*).
  - **Feminine:** most **-a** (*a casa*); **-ção/-são, -dade, -tude, -ie, -gem** (*a nação, a cidade, a juventude, a série, a viagem*).
  - Other endings must be memorized: *o mar, o lápis, o jornal* vs. *a flor, a cor, a dor, a raiz, a lei*; most **-ão** words are masculine (*o coração*), but *a mão, a razão, a opinião* are feminine.
- **Common-gender (sobrecomum):** one form for both sexes; only the article changes: *o/a colega, estudante, artista, jovem, dentista, cônjuge* [1].
- **Epicene nouns:** single grammatical gender regardless of sex — *a criança, a vítima, a testemunha, a pessoa*; modifiers stay feminine even for a male referent (*a vítima ficou ferida*) [1][2].
- **Superheteronyms:** suppletive pairs (*homem/mulher, pai/mãe, cavalo/égua*) [3].
- **Meaning changes with gender:** *o capital* (money) / *a capital* (city); *o rádio* (device) / *a rádio* (station); *o grama* (weight) / *a grama* (grass); *o cabeça* (leader) / *a cabeça* (body part); *o guia* (person) / *a guia* (document) [1][7].
- **Compound nouns:** verb+noun compounds are masculine (*o guarda-chuva, o beija-flor, o saca-rolhas, o vira-lata* — even though *flor, rolhas, lata* are feminine). Noun+noun compounds take the gender of the semantic head: *o peixe-espada, a palavra-chave, o carro-chefe, a couve-flor*; when the second element is the head: *a segunda-feira, o primeiro-ministro → a primeira-ministra* [1][6].

## 2. Articles and determiners [1][4]
- Definite: *o, os / a, as*; indefinite: *um, uns / uma, umas*. All determiners (possessives, demonstratives, quantifiers) agree: *meu/minha, este/esta, todo/toda, muito/muita, cujo/cuja*.
- **a → o rule:** the feminine article becomes **o** before feminine nouns beginning with stressed /a/: *o águia, o asa, o alma, o ama de leite* — but adjectives remain feminine (*o águia branca*), and demonstratives do not change (*esta águia*) [1][2].

## 3. Adjective agreement [1][2][4]
- Adjectives agree in **gender and number** with their noun: *o menino alto / a menina alta / os meninos altos / as meninas altas*.
- **Two-form** adjectives: *-o/-a* (*alto, bonito*). **Single-form** adjectives: *-e, -l, -z, -m, -s, -ar* (*grande, azul, feliz, jovem, popular*) — they vary only in number.
- **Compound adjectives:** only the last element inflects: *camisas verde-claras, olhos azul-escuros, relações greco-romanas, questões socioeconômicas*. Classic exception: *surdo-mudo → surdos-mudos* (both inflect) [1][2].
- **Multiple nouns:** same gender → that gender plural (*o pai e o filho são altos*); mixed genders → **masculine plural** (*João e Maria são altos*). Agreement with the nearest noun ("attractive agreement," *a mãe e o pai são altas*) occurs in speech but is nonstandard in formal writing [1][2].
- **Special cases:** *meio* is invariable as adverb (*elas estão meio cansadas*) but agrees as adjective (*meia hora*); *obrigado/obrigada* agrees with the speaker; *menos* and *alerta* are invariable; with *ser + proibido/necessário/vedado*, agreement occurs only if the noun has a determiner (*É proibido entrada* vs. *É proibida a entrada*) [1][6].
- Past participles agree with *ser/estar/ficar* (*as casas foram vendidas*) but stay invariable with *ter/haver* (*elas tinham chegado*) [2].

## 4. Generic masculine and mixed-gender phrases [1][3][5]
- The **masculine plural is the unmarked generic**: *os alunos*, *os brasileiros*, *todos* covers mixed groups; *pais* = parents, *irmãos* = siblings. This is the codified norm.
- Inclusive alternatives (*todos e todas*, *alunes*, *elu*) circulate in Brazilian institutional and activist usage but are **not recognized by normative grammars** as of standard codification [2][5][6].

## 5. Collective nouns [1][2][6]
- Collectives (*povo, multidão, equipe, família, turma, exército, elenco, bando*) are grammatically **singular**: *A multidão era enorme; A equipe está reunida* — never *A equipe venceram*.
- With a plural complement (*a maioria de, uma multidão de*), singular agreement is the formal norm (*A maioria dos alunos chegou*), but plural "notional" agreement (silepse) is widely accepted, especially when the complement names the individuals (*A maioria dos alunos chegaram; Uma multidão de fãs invadiram o campo*) [1][2][6].

## 6. Agreement with "pessoas" [1][3][7]
- *Pessoa* is a **feminine epicene noun**: it takes feminine agreement regardless of the sex of referents — *uma pessoa simpática* (man or woman), *as pessoas chegaram; todas estavam felizes*; pronouns referring back are feminine (*elas*).
- It is a regular plural noun, not a collective: agreement is always **plural** (*muitas pessoas chegaram*).
- To specify sex, use a phrase: *pessoa do sexo masculino/feminino*; the adjective still stays feminine (*ele é uma pessoa boa*) [1][3].

# Grammatical Gender Agreement in Portuguese — Research Summary

**Sources:** [1] Cunha & Cintra, *Nova Gramática do Português Contemporâneo* · [2] Bechara, *Moderna Gramática Portuguesa* · [3] Perini, *Modern Portuguese: A Reference Grammar* (2002) · [4] Whitlam, *Modern Brazilian Portuguese Grammar* · [5] Azevedo, *Portuguese: A Linguistic Introduction* · [6] Ciberdúvidas da Língua Portuguesa (ISCTE-IUL) · [7] *Dicionário Houaiss*

## 1. Noun gender (masculine/feminine) [1][3][7]
- Portuguese has **no neuter**; every noun is masculine or feminine, often by form:
  - **Masculine:** most **-o** words (*o livro*); Greek-origin **-ma** (*o problema, o sistema, o idioma, o clima*); most **-or** (*o escritor*).
  - **Feminine:** most **-a** (*a casa*); **-ção/-são, -dade, -tude, -ie, -gem** (*a nação, a cidade, a juventude, a série, a viagem*).
  - Other endings must be memorized: *o mar, o lápis, o jornal* vs. *a flor, a cor, a dor, a raiz, a lei*; most **-ão** words are masculine (*o coração*), but *a mão, a razão, a opinião* are feminine.
- **Common-gender (sobrecomum):** one form for both sexes; only the article changes: *o/a colega, estudante, artista, jovem, dentista, cônjuge* [1].
- **Epicene nouns:** single grammatical gender regardless of sex — *a criança, a vítima, a testemunha, a pessoa*; modifiers stay feminine even for a male referent (*a vítima ficou ferida*) [1][2].
- **Superheteronyms:** suppletive pairs (*homem/mulher, pai/mãe, cavalo/égua*) [3].
- **Meaning changes with gender:** *o capital* (money) / *a capital* (city); *o rádio* (device) / *a rádio* (station); *o grama* (weight) / *a grama* (grass); *o cabeça* (leader) / *a cabeça* (body part); *o guia* (person) / *a guia* (document) [1][7].
- **Compound nouns:** verb+noun compounds are masculine (*o guarda-chuva, o beija-flor, o saca-rolhas, o vira-lata* — even though *flor, rolhas, lata* are feminine). Noun+noun compounds take the gender of the semantic head: *o peixe-espada, a palavra-chave, o carro-chefe, a couve-flor*; when the second element is the head: *a segunda-feira, o primeiro-ministro → a primeira-ministra* [1][6].

## 2. Articles and determiners [1][4]
- Definite: *o, os / a, as*; indefinite: *um, uns / uma, umas*. All determiners (possessives, demonstratives, quantifiers) agree: *meu/minha, este/esta, todo/toda, muito/muita, cujo/cuja*.
- **a → o rule:** the feminine article becomes **o** before feminine nouns beginning with stressed /a/: *o águia, o asa, o alma, o ama de leite* — but adjectives remain feminine (*o águia branca*), and demonstratives do not change (*esta águia*) [1][2].

## 3. Adjective agreement [1][2][4]
- Adjectives agree in **gender and number** with their noun: *o menino alto / a menina alta / os meninos altos / as meninas altas*.
- **Two-form** adjectives: *-o/-a* (*alto, bonito*). **Single-form** adjectives: *-e, -l, -z, -m, -s, -ar* (*grande, azul, feliz, jovem, popular*) — they vary only in number.
- **Compound adjectives:** only the last element inflects: *camisas verde-claras, olhos azul-escuros, relações greco-romanas, questões socioeconômicas*. Classic exception: *surdo-mudo → surdos-mudos* (both inflect) [1][2].
- **Multiple nouns:** same gender → that gender plural (*o pai e o filho são altos*); mixed genders → **masculine plural** (*João e Maria são altos*). Agreement with the nearest noun ("attractive agreement," *a mãe e o pai são altas*) occurs in speech but is nonstandard in formal writing [1][2].
- **Special cases:** *meio* is invariable as adverb (*elas estão meio cansadas*) but agrees as adjective (*meia hora*); *obrigado/obrigada* agrees with the speaker; *menos* and *alerta* are invariable; with *ser + proibido/necessário/vedado*, agreement occurs only if the noun has a determiner (*É proibido entrada* vs. *É proibida a entrada*) [1][6].
- Past participles agree with *ser/estar/ficar* (*as casas foram vendidas*) but stay invariable with *ter/haver* (*elas tinham chegado*) [2].

## 4. Generic masculine and mixed-gender phrases [1][3][5]

## 1. Noun gender (masculine/feminine) [1][3][7]
- Portuguese has **no neuter**; every noun is masculine or feminine, often by form:
  - **Masculine:** most **-o** words (*o livro*); Greek-origin **-ma** (*o problema, o sistema, o idioma, o clima*); most **-or** (*o escritor*).

- **Common-gender (sobrecomum):** one form for both sexes; only the article changes: *o/a colega, estudante, artista, jovem, dentista, cônjuge* [1].
- **Epicene nouns:** single grammatical gender regardless of sex — *a criança, a vítima, a testemunha, a pessoa*; modifiers stay feminine even for a male referent (*a vítima ficou ferida*) [1][2].
- **Superheteronyms:** suppletive pairs (*homem/mulher, pai/mãe, cavalo/égua*) [3].
- **Meaning changes with gender:** *o capital* (money) / *a capital* (city); *o rádio* (device) / *a rádio* (station); *o grama* (weight) / *a grama* (grass); *o cabeça* (leader) / *a cabeça* (body part); *o guia* (person) / *a guia* (document) [1][7].

## 2. Articles and determiners [1][4]
- Definite: *o, os / a, as*; indefinite: *um, uns / uma, umas*. All determiners (possessives, demonstratives, quantifiers) agree: *meu/minha, este/esta, todo/toda, muito/muita, cujo/cuja*.

## 3. Adjective agreement [1][2][4]
- Adjectives agree in **gender and number** with their noun: *o menino alto / a menina alta / os meninos altos / as meninas altas*.
- **Two-form** adjectives: *-o/-a* (*alto, bonito*). **Single-form** adjectives: *-e, -l, -z, -m, -s, -ar* (*grande, azul, feliz, jovem, popular*) — they vary only in number.

- Past participles agree with *ser/estar/ficar* (*as casas foram vendidas*) but stay invariable with *ter/haver* (*elas tinham chegado*) [2].

- The **masculine plural is the unmarked generic**: *os alunos*, *os brasileiros*, *todos* covers mixed groups; *pais* = parents, *irmãos* = siblings. This is the codified norm.

## 5. Collective nouns [1][2][6]

message.content:
# CLDR Plural Rules for Portuguese (pt / pt-PT / pt-BR)

**Key fact:** CLDR has no separate plural data for pt-BR — it inherits from root `pt`. `pt`, `pt-PT`, and `pt-BR` share **identical cardinal rules**. Categories: **one, many, other** (`many` was added in CLDR 42 / ICU 72, Oct 2022, for compact/million-scale numbers) [1][3][7].

## 1. Cardinal rules [1][3]

```xml
<pluralRules locales="pt">
    <pluralRule count="one">i = 0..1</pluralRule>
    <pluralRule count="many">e = 0 and i != 0 and i % 1000000 = 0 and v = 0 or e != 0..5</pluralRule>
</pluralRules>
<!-- pt-PT is listed separately with identical rules; pt-BR inherits pt -->
```

Operand meanings per UTS #35 [4]: `i` = integer part, `v` = visible fraction digit count, `e` = compact exponent (0 if none).

- **one:** integer part is 0 or 1 → 0, 1, 0.5, 1.5, 1.99
- **many:** (no fraction, nonzero multiple of 1,000,000) OR (compact exponent ≥ 6) → 1000000, 2000000, 1M, 2B, 1e6
- **other:** everything else

## 2. Number examples (pt-BR formatting: comma decimal, dot thousands) [1][3]

| Number | Category | Why |
|---|---|---|
| 0 | one | i = 0 |
| 1 | one | i = 1 |
| 0,5 / 1,5 | one | i ≤ 1 |
| 2 / 100 / 2,5 | other | |
| 1.000.000 | many | multiple of 10⁶, v = 0 |
| 1.000.001 | other | not a multiple of 10⁶ |
| 1M (compact) | many | e = 6 |

Gotchas: **0 → "one"** and **1.5 → "one"** (Portuguese uses singular below 2: "1,5 item"). Use an explicit `=0` selector if you need special zero handling.

## 3. Ordinal rules [2][3]

```xml
<pluralRules locales="pt">
    <pluralRule count="one">n = 1</pluralRule>
</pluralRules>
```

| Number | Category | Example |
|---|---|---|
| 1 | one | 1º (primeiro) |
| 2, 3, 11, 1.5 | other | 2º, 3º, 11º |

(Gender suffix º/ª is not captured by plural categories.)

## 4. ICU MessageFormat syntax for pt-BR [5]

```
{n, plural,
  =0 {nenhum resultado}
  one {# resultado}
  many {# de resultados}
  other {# resultados}}
```

Outputs: `1 → "1 resultado"` · `2 → "2 resultados"` · `1,5 → "1,5 resultado"` · `1000000 → "1.000.000 de resultados"` · `0 → "nenhum resultado"` (or "0 resultado" without `=0`)

```java
// Java (ICU4J)
MessageFormat mf = new MessageFormat(
    "{n, plural, one {# item} many {# de itens} other {# itens}}",
    Locale.forLanguageTag("pt-BR"));
PluralRules rules = PluralRules.forLocale(ULocale.forLanguageTag("pt-BR"));
rules.select(0);         // "one"
rules.select(1_000_000); // "many"
```

```js
// JavaScript
new Intl.PluralRules('pt-BR').select(1);        // "one"
new Intl.PluralRules('pt-BR').select(1000000);  // "many"
new Intl.PluralRules('pt-BR', {type:'ordinal'}).select(1); // "one"
```

Ordinals in MessageFormat: `{pos, selectordinal, one {#º lugar} other {#º lugar}}` → 1 → "1º lugar", 2 → "2º lugar".

## 5. Notes

- `many` requires CLDR 42+ data (ICU 72+, modern browsers/Node); older runtimes silently never select it [7].
- `#` renders the number locale-formatted (e.g., "1,5").
- pt-PT differs from pt only in **pluralRanges** (range combination resolution, e.g. "1–2 …"), not in cardinal/ordinal categories [6].

## Sources
[1] CLDR `common/supplemental/plurals.xml` (cardinal rules) · [2] CLDR `common/supplemental/ordinals.xml` · [3] CLDR Language Plural Rules chart, unicode.org/cldr/charts/latest/supplemental/language_plural_rules.html · [4] UTS #35 LDML Part 3: Numbers, "Language Plural Rules" (tr35-numbers.html) · [5] ICU MessageFormat/PluralFormat docs, unicode.org/icu/userguide/format_parse/messages · [6] CLDR `common/supplemental/pluralRanges.xml` · [7] CLDR 42 release notes (many-category addition), cldr.unicode.org/index/downloads/cldr-42

# CLDR Plural Rules for Portuguese (pt / pt-PT / pt-BR)

**Key fact:** CLDR has no separate plural data for pt-BR — it inherits from root `pt`. `pt`, `pt-PT`, and `pt-BR` share **identical cardinal rules**. Categories: **one, many, other** (`many` was added in CLDR 42 / ICU 72, Oct 2022, for compact/million-scale numbers) [1][3][7].

## 1. Cardinal rules [1][3]

```xml
<pluralRules locales="pt">
    <pluralRule count="one">i = 0..1</pluralRule>
    <pluralRule count="many">e = 0 and i != 0 and i % 1000000 = 0 and v = 0 or e != 0..5</pluralRule>
</pluralRules>
<!-- pt-PT is listed separately with identical rules; pt-BR inherits pt -->
```

Operand meanings per UTS #35 [4]: `i` = integer part, `v` = visible fraction digit count, `e` = compact exponent (0 if none).

- **one:** integer part is 0 or 1 → 0, 1, 0.5, 1.5, 1.99
- **many:** (no fraction, nonzero multiple of 1,000,000) OR (compact exponent ≥ 6) → 1000000, 2000000, 1M, 2B, 1e6
- **other:** everything else

## 2. Number examples (pt-BR formatting: comma decimal, dot thousands) [1][3]

| Number | Category | Why |
|---|---|---|
| 0 | one | i = 0 |
| 1 | one | i = 1 |
| 0,5 / 1,5 | one | i ≤ 1 |
| 2 / 100 / 2,5 | other | |
| 1.000.000 | many | multiple of 10⁶, v = 0 |
| 1.000.001 | other | not a multiple of 10⁶ |
| 1M (compact) | many | e = 6 |

Gotchas: **0 → "one"** and **1.5 → "one"** (Portuguese uses singular below 2: "1,5 item"). Use an explicit `=0` selector if you need special zero handling.

## 3. Ordinal rules [2][3]

```xml
<pluralRules locales="pt">
    <pluralRule count="one">n = 1</pluralRule>
</pluralRules>
```

| Number | Category | Example |
|---|---|---|
| 1 | one | 1º (primeiro) |
| 2, 3, 11, 1.5 | other | 2º, 3º, 11º |

(Gender suffix º/ª is not captured by plural categories.)

## 4. ICU MessageFormat syntax for pt-BR [5]

```
{n, plural,
  =0 {nenhum resultado}
  one {# resultado}
  many {# de resultados}
  other {# resultados}}
```

Outputs: `1 → "1 resultado"` · `2 → "2 resultados"` · `1,5 → "1,5 resultado"` · `1000000 → "1.000.000 de resultados"` · `0 → "nenhum resultado"` (or "0 resultado" without `=0`)

```java
// Java (ICU4J)
MessageFormat mf = new MessageFormat(
    "{n, plural, one {# item} many {# de itens} other {# itens}}",
    Locale.forLanguageTag("pt-BR"));
PluralRules rules = PluralRules.forLocale(ULocale.forLanguageTag("pt-BR"));
rules.select(0);         // "one"
rules.select(1_000_000); // "many"
```

```js
// JavaScript
new Intl.PluralRules('pt-BR').select(1);        // "one"
new Intl.PluralRules('pt-BR').select(1000000);  // "many"
new Intl.PluralRules('pt-BR', {type:'ordinal'}).select(1); // "one"
```

Ordinals in MessageFormat: `{pos, selectordinal, one {#º lugar} other {#º lugar}}` → 1 → "1º lugar", 2 → "2º lugar".

## 5. Notes

- `many` requires CLDR 42+ data (ICU 72+, modern browsers/Node); older runtimes silently never select it [7].
- `#` renders the number locale-formatted (e.g., "1,5").
- pt-PT differs from pt only in **pluralRanges** (range combination resolution, e.g. "1–2 …"), not in cardinal/ordinal categories [6].

## Sources
[1] CLDR `common/supplemental/plurals.xml` (cardinal rules) · [2] CLDR `common/supplemental/ordinals.xml` · [3] CLDR Language Plural Rules chart, unicode.org/cldr/charts/latest/supplemental/language_plural_rules.html · [4] UTS #35 LDML Part 3: Numbers, "Language Plural Rules" (tr35-numbers.html) · [5] ICU MessageFormat/PluralFormat docs, unicode.org/icu/userguide/format_parse/messages · [6] CLDR `common/supplemental/pluralRanges.xml` · [7] CLDR 42 release notes (many-category addition), cldr.unicode.org/index/downloads/cldr-42
